module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 906

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/906](https://www.erdosproblems.com/906)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos906

/-- Does there exists an entire non-zero transcendental function `f : ℂ → ℂ` such that for any
sequence `n₀ < n₁ < ...`, `{ z | ∃ k, iteratedDeriv (n k) f z = 0 }` is dense. -/
@[category research open, AMS 30]
theorem erdos_906 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ f : ℂ → ℂ, Transcendental (Polynomial ℂ) f ∧
    Differentiable ℂ f ∧ ∀ n : ℕ → ℕ, StrictMono n →
    Dense { z | ∃ k, iteratedDeriv (n k) f z = 0 } := by
  sorry

end Erdos906

reformulations.difference: The source asks about an "entire non-zero function f: ℂ → ℂ". The Lean asks for `Transcendental (Polynomial ℂ) f ∧ Differentiable ℂ f`. Here `Transcendental ℂ[X] f` uses the repository instance `Polynomial.instAlgebraPi`, where `algebraMap p = fun z => p.eval z`. It means that no nonzero P ∈ ℂ[X][Y] has P(z, f z) = 0 for all z. This follows the source's own remark: the literal problem is trivial for polynomials, "so presumably it is intended the function f is transcendental".
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For entire f, `Transcendental ℂ[X] f` holds exactly when f is not a polynomial function, which is the usual meaning of "transcendental entire function". (1) A polynomial function q is algebraic: take P = Y − C q. (2) Conversely, suppose f is entire and P(z, f z) ≡ 0 with P ≠ 0. P cannot have Y-degree 0, since a nonzero polynomial does not vanish on all of ℂ. So P has leading coefficient a_d(z) ≠ 0 with d ≥ 1. Cauchy's root bound gives |f(z)| ≤ 1 + max_i |a_i(z)/a_d(z)| = O(|z|^m) for large |z|. By the Cauchy estimates, f is then a polynomial. Transcendence also implies f ≠ 0, so the source's "non-zero" is covered. Without the transcendence hypothesis the right-hand side is trivially true: a nonzero constant has every derivative of order ≥ 1 identically zero, so the zero set is all of ℂ (proved in Lean). So the Lean states the non-trivial version the source says is intended. Under the other literal reading, where the roots of the zero function are ignored, polynomials fail and the problem is again equivalent to the transcendental version.

reformulations.difference: The source quantifies over sequences n₁ < n₂ < ⋯ indexed from 1, with orders presumably positive. The Lean quantifies over every `StrictMono n : ℕ → ℕ`, indexed from 0, so `n 0 = 0` is allowed and f itself (the derivative of order 0) can contribute zeros.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: If the Lean condition holds for all strictly increasing sequences in ℕ, it holds in particular for those with positive values. Conversely, take any strictly increasing n. Its tail k ↦ n (k+1) is strictly increasing with values ≥ 1. The union of zero sets along the tail is contained in the union for n, and a superset of a dense set is dense. Proved in Lean (`Dense.mono` on the tail). I also proved in Lean that the Lean condition is equivalent to the forum's 'cofinite hitting' reformulation: for every nonempty open U, eventually every f^{(m)} has a zero in U.

review.notes:
The file has one declaration, `Erdos906.erdos_906 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ f : ℂ → ℂ, Transcendental ℂ[X] f ∧ Differentiable ℂ f ∧ ∀ n, StrictMono n → Dense {z | ∃ k, iteratedDeriv (n k) f z = 0}`.

Source wording. It matches the question as posed in all three sources:
- erdosproblems.com/906: "Is there an entire non-zero function f such that, for any infinite sequence n₁<n₂<⋯, the set {z : f^{(n_k)}(z)=0 for some k≥1} is everywhere dense?"
- [Er82e] p. 72: "for every infinite sequence of integers n₁<n₂<⋯ the set ⋃ S_{n_i} is everywhere dense, where S_n is the set of roots of f^{(n)}(z)".
- [Er56d] English summary: "Does there exist an entire function f(z), so that for every sequence n₁<n₂<… the union of the set of all the roots of f^{(n_k)}(z)=0 is everywhere dense in the plane".

Statement checks. The quantifier order is right: ∃ f, then ∀ sequences. `Dense` is taken in the standard topology on ℂ. The zero set is the union over k. `answer(sorry)` sits in front of a closed proposition. The transcendence restriction follows the site's explicit remark that the literal version is trivial for polynomials.

Lean checks (scratch files in /workspace/review/; all compile, standard axioms only):
- Polynomial functions are not `Transcendental ℂ[X]`.
- `Transcendental ℂ[X] f → f ≠ 0`.
- `IsAlgebraic ℂ[X] f ↔ ∃ P ≠ 0, ∀ z, aevalAeval z (f z) P = 0`.
- `Transcendental ℂ[X] Complex.exp` is proved (via 2πi-periodicity), so the existential's hypotheses are satisfiable. `exp` itself is no witness, since its derivatives never vanish.
- Without transcendence the right-hand side is trivially true (take a constant).
- The ℕ-indexing and the forum's cofinite reformulation are both equivalent to the Lean condition.

No trivial proof or refutation is available.

Status. The file says `research open`, and erdosproblems.com still shows OPEN (page last edited 1 Oct 2025, accessed 2026-09-23); the teorth database also says open. So I record no status issue. Maintainers may want to watch the forum, though. There are unverified affirmative proof sketches from April 2026 (random Fock/Gaussian entire functions), plus two 'full proof' claims with external Lean developments: E. Hou (2026-07-21) and Z. He (2026-09-17). The site has not accepted either. If one is accepted, the answer would be `answer(True)`, because both claims prove exactly the cofinite property, which I showed is equivalent to the Lean right-hand side.

Minor, not a finding. The theorem docstring has a grammar slip ("Does there exists") and uses code formatting rather than LaTeX. It does not say why "transcendental" replaces the source's "non-zero". The mathematics is unaffected.
